subject: History
description: Rock and pillar edicts of Emperor Ashoka

questions.stem: Most of Ashoka's Rock and Pillar edicts were written in which script?
questions.explanation: Most Ashokan edicts are in Brahmi script (reading left to right) — used for Prakrit, the spoken language. Some NW edicts use Kharoshthi (right to left, Aramaic-derived); two bilinguals in Greek / Aramaic (Kandahar, in modern Afghanistan). Brahmi was deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837, unlocking the edicts. Brahmi is the ancestor of most Indian scripts, including Devanagari (a later medieval script).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Ashokan pillar which bears the four-lion capital now used as India's national emblem is at:
questions.explanation: The Lion Capital at Sarnath — adopted as India's state emblem on 26 January 1950 — has four Asiatic lions back-to-back on an abacus with an elephant, horse, bull and lion (each representing a direction). The 'Satyameva Jayate' motto below is from the Mundaka Upanishad. Sanchi has its own great Stupa, and Vaishali has the single-lion pillar.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The 13th Major Rock Edict of Ashoka is chiefly about:

options.option_text: The Kalinga War and Ashoka's remorse

questions.explanation: The 13th Rock Edict — Ashoka's most famous — describes the bloodshed of the Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE), 100,000 killed and many more deported, and his resulting remorse, his adoption of dhamma-vijaya (conquest by righteousness). It also names 5 Hellenistic kings (Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus Gonatas, Magas of Cyrene, Alexander of Epirus) to whom he sent missions, establishing the date of Ashoka's reign.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Ashokan edicts were deciphered in 1837 by:
questions.explanation: James Prinsep (Assay Master at the Calcutta Mint) cracked the Brahmi script in 1837, making the Ashokan edicts readable for the first time in nearly two millennia. Sir William Jones (1746-94) founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal (1784). Alexander Cunningham (1814-93) was the first DG of the Archaeological Survey of India. Charles Wilkins first translated the Bhagavad Gita into English (1785).
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: Ashokan edicts are mostly written in which language family?
questions.explanation: Most Ashokan edicts are in varieties of Prakrit — the Middle Indo-Aryan spoken languages of the time. The Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra edicts (both in modern Pakistan) are in Prakrit but in Kharoshthi script. Two bilinguals in Aramaic + Greek (Kandahar). Not Sanskrit (the scholarly language). Pali is a specific Prakrit — Ashokan edicts are not, strictly speaking, in Pali.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The Ashokan pillar at Lumbini marks:

options.option_text: The first sermon of the Buddha

questions.explanation: The Lumbini Pillar (in modern Nepal) records Ashoka's visit in the 21st year of his reign to honour the Buddha's birthplace and exempts Lumbini from most taxes. Bodh Gaya — enlightenment; Sarnath — first sermon; Kushinagar — mahaparinirvana. Lumbini has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997.
questions.subject: History

questions.stem: The original name of Emperor Ashoka — based on inscriptions and literature — was:
questions.explanation: 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' ('Beloved of the gods, he who looks on lovingly') is the title Ashoka uses for himself in his edicts. The name 'Ashoka' is known from Buddhist texts (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa of Sri Lanka). The Maski Edict (Karnataka) is the crucial one that contains BOTH names and thus confirms they refer to the same person. Chandragupta — founder of the Mauryan dynasty. Bimbisara — Haryanka ruler of Magadha (6th century BCE). Harshavardhana — 7th-century emperor.
